article_title: Improving Access to Interactive, Mother-Tongue Digital Science Content for Early Grade Learners in Rural Haiti

title: Three-component pilot model combining infrastructure and technology, Creole digital content, and professional development with coaching
description: The pilot model organizes implementation into three components. improved learning outcomes in Creole science content

article_title: Magnet Schools and Metropolitan Civil Rights Planning: A Strategy to Revitalize and Stabilize Distressed Communities
citation: Orfield, M., & Stancil, W. (2022). Magnet schools and metropolitan civil rights planning: A strategy to revitalize and stabilize distressed communities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/197.312
title: Combined geographic-zone and open-enrollment attendance policy for revitalization magnets
description: A magnet attendance design combining a residential attendance boundary with voluntary regional open enrollment, so the school both serves its immediate neighborhood and draws integrating families from the wider region. The report describes "implementing an attendance policy in which 50% of a school's enrollment is drawn from a particular geographic zone and 50% is drawn as open enrollment from the larger region." In a low-income segregated area, zone students are likely nonwhite and lower-income while open-enrollment students are more likely white and affluent, and strong demand can make the attendance zone housing attractive, supporting residential integration.
requirements: Strong demand for magnet seats so families seek housing in the geographic attendance zone
constraints: The report warns poorly designed magnets can lose their ability to attract enrollment, and high-demand schools risk becoming heavily white and affluent without enrollment-weighting policies
target_learners: K-12 students in racially and economically segregated urban neighborhoods
target_learning_goals: School integration
Neighborhood revitalization through school quality
examples: The report cites successful magnets in the Hartford, CT, and San Antonio, TX, regions that weight enrollment by socioeconomic strata

article_title: AI Advice Suppresses People's Willingness to Say \"I Don't Know\", Even When the Advice Is Wrong and Accuracy Is Incentivized
citation: Chiara Marcoccia, Walter Quattrociocchi, Valerio Capraro. (2026). AI advice suppresses people's willingness to say "I don't know", even when the advice is wrong and accuracy is incentivized. https://osf.io/nwx6r/overview?view_only=a03ae0ca587c4c84a442c44d55ab97b6
title: Hallucination-inducing film-detail question set with pre-generated incorrect AI responses
description: A six-question instrument about fine visual details of films (e.g., Agatha's hairstyle in The Grand Budapest Hotel), designed, in the article's words, to be "both hard for participants to answer and likely to induce hallucinations (i.e., fabricated answers)" from the LLM used, Step 3.5 Flash. Because the advice was usually wrong, any drop in suspension cannot be read as sensible delegation to a reliable tool. In later studies, AI replies were drawn at random from pre-recorded outputs so every advice-seeker received a complete, well-formed answer.
requirements: Questions about details minor enough to be largely absent from online text, so that language models trained on such text fabricate answers
Pre-generated responses per question so displayed advice is complete and constant across participants
constraints: The questions engineer an almost-always-wrong AI, so the paradigm isolates unreliable advice; the article states it is untested whether suspension collapses equally with usually-correct advice
target_learners: Adult crowdworkers (Prolific, US-based)
target_learning_goals: Measuring judgment suspension, correctness, confidence, and AI-advice seeking under uncertain knowledge
examples: Study 1b displayed one of three pre-recorded Step 3.5 Flash responses per question, drawn at random, to eliminate live-query failures.

article_title: From Prompt to Embodied Simulation: Using Generative AI to Create AR Physics Learning Tools
citation: Ofek Levy, Joshua Glazer, Noah D. Finkelstein, and Yossi Ben-Zion. (2026). From Prompt to Embodied Simulation: Using Generative AI to Create AR Physics Learning Tools. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22From+Prompt+to+Embodied+Simulation%22
title: Hand-controlled AR electromagnetism simulations: fingertip charge with field grid, two-charge combined field, and right-hand rule on the student's own hand
description: Three simulations built from the same four-element prompt, with full prompts given in the online appendix. In the first, "the tip of the index finger is an electric charge, and a three-dimensional grid of arrows, showing the electric field of the charge, fills the space around the student"; arrows are longer near the charge and shorter farther away. In the second, each index finger is a charge of opposite sign and bringing the hands together concentrates the combined field. In the third, "the right-hand rule is drawn on the student's own hand: three arrows, force, velocity, and field, anchored to three fingers and rotating with the hand," displayed without mirroring so handedness is preserved.
requirements: MediaPipe Hands and Three.js; for the right-hand-rule simulation the camera feed must not be mirrored, since mirroring reverses handedness and would invert the rule being taught
constraints: The visualizations are qualitative teaching representations; the wave-and-lamp simulation is explicitly not a quantitative model of an electromagnetic field
target_learners: introductory physics students
teachers of electromagnetism
target_learning_goals: electric fields of point charges
field superposition of two charges
the right-hand rule for the magnetic force F = qv × B
examples: Appendix Prompts A, B, and C give the complete prompts for the single charge, two-charge, and right-hand-rule simulations respectively

article_title: Unpacking Interaction Profiles and Strategies in Human-AI Collaborative Problem Solving: A Cognitive Distribution and Regulation Perspective
citation: Zhanxin Hao, Xiaobo Liu, Jiaxin Fan, Yun Long, Jifan Yu, Wenli Chen, Yu Zhang. (2025). Unpacking Interaction Profiles and Strategies in Human-AI Collaborative Problem Solving: A Cognitive Distribution and Regulation Perspective. https://www.maic.chat
title: HA-CORD: Human-AI Cognitive and Regulatory Distribution model
description: The HA-CORD model integrates distributed cognition theory with regulation-of-learning theories (self-regulation, co-regulation, socially-shared regulation) to explain human-AI collaborative problem solving. The article states: "we propose a more integrated framework for AI-supported collaborative problem solving, one that explains both how cognitive work is distributed and how that distribution is dynamically regulated by human and AI agents." It treats cognitive offloading and scaffolding alongside metacognitive monitoring and model adaptation, and organizes the three empirical profiles (DR, CI, DE) along axes of distributed cognition and distributed regulation.
requirements: Dialogue-level coding of human-AI interaction to observe cognitive distribution and regulatory moves
constraints: The article notes classical distributed cognition pays less explicit attention to metacognitive activities within individual human members, which the regulation layer is intended to address
target_learners: college students collaborating with AI agents
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving
metacognitive regulation of learning
examples: The three identified profiles were mapped onto the model as a spectrum from distributed cognition with metacognitive detachment (DR) to human-centered cognition with deepest regulation (CI), with DE as a transitional middle ground

article_title: Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction
citation: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309
title: Hazel Prover, a web-based classroom proof assistant for equational and inductive reasoning about typed functional programs
description: Hazel Prover is "implemented as an extension to Hazel, a live typed functional programming environment". Students interleave programs and theorem specifications in the Hazel editor; theorem constructs appear as proof obligations at the bottom of the screen. Students highlight sub-expressions and choose to rewrite or perform an induction, with evaluation steps, algebra steps checked by an external computer algebra checker, and assumption steps. There is no proof-assistant-specific syntax; all proof logic is expressed via a graphical user interface, and proofs are laid out similarly to written proofs.
requirements: Installation and setup should be straightforward, and the tool should require minimal training specific to the tool, per the article's Criteria 6 and 7.
constraints: The algebra solver is given access only to arithmetic and arithmetic operators, leaving Hazel's control flow and list primitives opaque, so students cannot simply rewrite the entire proposition to true.
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate and graduate programming languages students
target_learning_goals: step-by-step equational and inductive reasoning about functional programs
examples: In the second deployment one exercise required students to write their own implementation of Peano multiplication and prove it correct.
key_sources: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309

article_title: Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming
citation: Iyiola E. Olatunji, Alberick Euraste Djire, Jacques Klein, and Tegawendé F. Bissyandé. 2026. Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming. Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3834554
title: Handoff design space for AI coding assistants: six handoff types from direct transfer to provenance marking
description: Table 1 enumerates the handoff design space the paper proposes for AI coding assistants: Direct (code transfers immediately with no intervention), Explanation-first (assistant provides reasoning before code, promoting inspection), Soft-barrier (code is readable but naive copy-paste execution fails), Review-gated (transfer requires a summary, test, or confirmation step), Test-gated (insertion is blocked until the learner runs or writes tests), and Provenance-marked (generated code carries metadata for attribution or auditing). These types could form a policy layer between an LLM and an IDE, LMS, or repository.

constraints: The paper studies only one point in this design space (soft-barrier handoff) technically

professional software developers
target_learning_goals: shaping how generated code is transferred, inspected, tested, or attributed
examples: Campus-managed assistants such as UniGPT-style services could support explanation-first, test-gated, or soft-barrier modes

article_title: A Hybrid Reasoning Framework for Artificial Intelligence Assessment Rubric Generation in Human and Automated Contexts: Evidence from an Undergraduate Programming Course
citation: Pedro C. Mendonça, Filipe Quintal, Mário Figueiredo, Karolina Baras, Fábio Mendonça. (2026). A hybrid reasoning framework for artificial intelligence assessment rubric generation in human and automated contexts: Evidence from an undergraduate programming course. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100663
title: HARMOGEN-R: a two-stage hybrid framework for AI rubric generation with reasoning-enhanced generation and low-temperature synthesis
description: HARMOGEN-R (Hybrid Assessment Rubric Model Generation with Reasoning) is a two-stage rubric generation pipeline. In stage one, reasoning-capable LLMs generate several candidate rubrics under a high temperature setting "to promote variation in criterion formulation and scoring structure"; in stage two, a synthesis model from the same provider family consolidates the candidates into a single rubric at low temperature (T = 1.0 for generation, T = 0.1 for synthesis). It supports a structured mode, in which predefined criteria and point allocations from the human baseline are supplied, and a free-form mode, in which the model defines criteria autonomously. Implemented with OpenAI (o3-mini, GPT-4o) and DeepSeek (deepseek-r1-distill-llama-70b, deepseek-chat) families, it produced four AI rubric variants per assessment for comparison against a human-created baseline.
requirements: Access to hosted API endpoints for both generation and evaluation stages; each initial generation prompt includes the assessment question, an exemplar correct response, two generic rubric examples, and explicit score-distribution instructions
constraints: The study states its benchmark human rubric's role should be interpreted in operational rather than absolute terms, since no external formal validation of rubric quality was performed
All models were accessed through hosted API endpoints; no model was deployed on institutional infrastructure
target_learners: Undergraduate computer engineering students in first-year programming courses
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment of open-ended programming and short-answer responses in data structures and algorithms
examples: For each rubric condition the initial model generated three independent candidate rubrics, merged during synthesis into a single final version, across three formative programming assignments

article_title: Assessing the proficiency of large language models in automatic feedback generation: An evaluation study
citation: Wei Dai, Yi-Shan Tsai, Jionghao Lin, Ahmad Aldino, Hua Jin, Tongguang Li, Dragan Gašević, Guanliang Chen. (2023). Assessing the Proficiency of Large Language Models in Automatic Feedback Generation: An Evaluation Study. Preprint submitted to Elsevier. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Assessing+the+Proficiency+of+Large+Language+Models+in+Automatic+Feedback+Generation
title: Hattie and Timperley's feedback model: three dimensions (feeding up, feeding back, feeding forward) and four levels (task, process, self-regulation, self)
description: The article adopts this theoretical framework to analyse the effectiveness of textual feedback. It "categorized effective feedback into three dimensions (i.e., feeding up, feeding back and feeding forward) and four-level focuses (i.e., task, process, self-regulatory, and self )". Feeding up tells students where they are going; feeding back answers how they are going; feeding forward addresses where to go next. The authors chose it because it "has been adopted widely in previous research to analyse textual feedback", unlike Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's principles judged too general.
requirements: Annotators trained in the framework's three dimensions and four levels to label feedback content
constraints: The article notes effectiveness of feedback goes beyond the content coverage of feedback, so this single framework does not capture relational or feedback-literacy dimensions
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: assessment feedback quality on writing tasks
examples: Two experts annotated 309 feedback pieces using the framework's dimensions and levels, with a third expert resolving inconsistencies

article_title: Handwriting Fluency in Children
citation: Wicki, Werner; Hurschler Lichtsteiner, Sibylle; Saxer Geiger, Andrea; Müller, Marianne (2014). Handwriting fluency in children. Swiss Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1024/1421-0185/a000127
title: Cognitive-resource-saving account of handwriting automaticity
description: The article frames its findings with theories holding that when handwriting becomes automatic, fewer cognitive resources are consumed by the mechanics of writing, freeing capacity for higher-level composition processes such as spelling and text generation. The authors state: "The results are discussed with respect to theories that assume that the automaticity of handwriting is associated with saving cognitive resources." The SEM finding that automaticity predicts orthographic skills independently of visual-motor integration is interpreted in this light.
requirements: Handwriting must reach a level of automaticity for resource savings to be available to other writing processes
constraints: Evidence in this article is cross-sectional and correlational, so the direction of the resource-saving mechanism is not tested
target_learners: children in primary/elementary school (fourth graders)
target_learning_goals: written composition, spelling and orthographic skills
examples: The study measured automaticity of handwriting, stroke pressure, and stroke frequency on a digitizing tablet during a copying task.

article_title: Conceptualizing the intersubjective group
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4
title: Habermas's ideal speech situation and three-worlds distinction as conditions for intersubjectivity in CSCL
description: Drawing on Hammond's introduction of Habermas, the article presents the ideal speech situation—an underlying assumption that "there is no other force of persuasion at work than that of the better argument and no other motivation than the cooperative search for truth"—as a standard for judging knowledge building in chats, forums, or Wikipedia, even though the ideal is never fully achievable. Habermas also distinguishes objective, social, and subjective worlds, each with different validity criteria, giving analysts leverage to apply appropriate evaluative criteria to each level of a team's collaborative work.
requirements: Discourse participants must assume cooperative truth-seeking rather than force or authority as grounds for persuasion
constraints: The ideal speech situation "is never in fact achievable"; other forces and motivations are always present
target_learners: students collaborating online; researchers analyzing collaborative discourse
target_learning_goals: intersubjective meaning making and collaborative knowledge building

citation: Tatiana Íñiguez-Berrozpe, Carmen Elboj-Saso, Francesco Marcaletti, Pablo Bautista-Alcaine. (2025). title: Four-question hate speech case with a unified level-ordered scoring rubric (kappa 0.841)
description: The study used four quantitative questions on the María case, scored on level-ordered rubrics grounded in Kohlberg's moral development theory and models of empathic concern and digital citizenship. "A total of 1400 responses out of the 4508 submitted by participants were provided to each of the trained coders", coded blind to conditions and hypotheses, with Cohen's kappa of 0.841 indicating almost perfect agreement and disagreements resolved by consensus. Questions assessed perceived legitimacy of defending an influencer, awareness of who is harmed, who benefits, and prosocial action readiness on a 1–6 scale.

target_learning_goals: Ethical reasoning about online hate speech
moral responsibility
empathy and prosocial action readiness
examples: Question 4 ranged from total defense of the influencer (answer 1) to reporting the account for spreading hate speech (answer 6)

article_title: Investigating Students’ Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks
citation: Parks, T., Shehab, S., & Mercier, E. (2026). Investigating Students' Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09816-0
title: Include hard scaffolds in the design of ill-structured tasks for collaborative problem solving in higher education STEM classrooms
description: Hard scaffolds are static supports planned in advance (question prompts, checklists, concept maps) that direct students toward anticipated difficulties. This study shows that embedding explicit prompts for exploring, planning, and evaluating into ill-structured engineering tasks shifts group interactions toward a more balanced distribution of the four problem-solving processes and raises final solution quality. The authors conclude these findings "support the need to include hard scaffolds in the design of ill-structured tasks for collaborative problem solving in higher education STEM classrooms."
requirements: Tasks must be ill-structured and designed for face-to-face collaborative problem solving
Scaffolds must explicitly prompt underused processes (P1, P2, P4) rather than only solution attempts
constraints: Scaffold transfer to non-scaffolded tasks remains unresolved; the article notes scaffolding fading research suggests strategic removal is needed
Study did not control for perceived task difficulty or time between tasks
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in required introductory courses
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving processes (exploring, planning, solving, evaluating) in ill-structured engineering tasks
examples: The scaffolded task included a marked area for constructing a free body diagram (P1), a prompt to plan the type of loading (P2), and explicit direction to evaluate the factor of safety (P4), presented on synchronized digital tablets

article_title: Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit
citation: Ann-Kathrin Krause, Jasmin Breitwieser, Garvin Brod. (2025). Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10087-3
title: Habit-based lens on learning strategy use: strategies can be driven by automatic cue-response associations alongside deliberate regulation
description: The article proposes framing learning strategy use through modern habit theory, in which a habit is "a learned association between a contextual cue and a behavioral response" that develops through repeated cue-behavior pairing. Drawing on dual-process models, it argues strategy use can stem from both controlled, reasoned decisions and automatic, cue-driven habitual impulses. The lens complements self-regulated learning models, which acknowledge automaticity but treat automatic routines as readily adjustable, whereas habits are cue-bound and hard to disrupt.
requirements: Repeated performance of the behavior in a stable context with a salient cue for a habit to form
constraints: The authors note habitual behavior exists on a continuum and is not necessarily non-intentional or unconscious
target_learners: students in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: self-regulated use of effective cognitive learning strategies for long-term retention
examples: The article illustrates the lens with highlighting while reading: opening a text becomes the cue that triggers the impulse to grab a pencil and highlight, even though highlighting may not enhance long-term retention
key_sources: Ann-Kathrin Krause, Jasmin Breitwieser, Garvin Brod. (2025). Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10087-3

article_title: Some results of practice in addition under school conditions.
citation: H. H. Hahn and E. L. Thorndike. (1914). Some Results of Practice in Addition Under School Conditions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Volume V, Number 2. https://www.google.com/search?q=Hahn+Thorndike+1914+Some+Results+of+Practice+in+Addition+Under+School+Conditions
title: Hahn-Thorndike school addition practice experiment with self-competition and no-practice control groups
description: A school-based experiment in which pupils in grades 4 through 7 added columns, each of ten one-place numbers, as rapidly as was consistent with accuracy. Each pupil competed against his own record: "Each child was led to compete with his own past record—was told repeatedly 'to beat himself.'" Seven sheets of forty-eight columns of equal difficulty were used; practice groups took an initial 15-minute test, 90 minutes of practice in periods from 5 to 22.5 minutes, and a final test, while control groups took only the two tests.

constraints: Out-of-school practice was not prevented and could not be detected or subtracted from the obtained results
target_learners: school pupils in grades 4-7
target_learning_goals: speed and accuracy in adding columns of one-place numbers
examples: Practice periods of 5, 7.5, 10, 15, 20 and 22.5 minutes were assigned to different groups across an October-November schedule

article_title: Tests of applicants for admission to University of Minnesota Medical School.

description: The battery used for 1916 medical school applicants comprised an omnibus test "fashioned after the one reported by Scott," arranged in triplicate to prevent communication between groups tested on different days, and sets of the Thorndike Improved Scale for Reading Ability, Scale Alpha 2. Both tests were given at one sitting, scored for rate and quality, with each omnibus error penalized by adding ten seconds to raw time to give a weighted time. The article states the two tests occupied two examiners for not to exceed one and one-half hours and that a hundred applicants may be examined at a sitting.

article_title: Habituation as an adaptive shift in response strategy mediated by neuropeptides
citation: Evan L. Ardiel, Alex J. Yu, Andrew C. Giles and Catharine H. Rankin. (2017). Habituation as an adaptive shift in response strategy mediated by neuropeptides. npj Science of Learning 2:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0011-8
title: Habituation to noxious stimuli as a PDF-orchestrated shift in behavioral strategy from backward escape to forward dispersal
description: The article proposes that habituation is not simply response decrement but part of a coordinated shift in behavioral strategy: reversal responses are largely maintained while their duration shortens and latency increases, and forward locomotion between responses increases, promoting dispersal from a dangerous locale. It interprets this within the dual-process theory of habituation, in which "each stimulus induces both local circuit habituation and organism-wide sensitization," so that coincident habituation and sensitization form an optimal escape strategy balancing immediate threat evasion against longer-term evacuation, resonating with Bolles's species-specific defense responses.
requirements: Repeated aversive stimulation detectable by a nociceptive circuit
Multiple behavioral metrics measured in an intact, freely moving animal
constraints: The authors state this interpretation is not expected to generalize to every habituating behavior
target_learners: C. elegans adults
target_learning_goals: Habituation to repeated noxious stimulation
examples: Detailed behavioral analysis during learning acquisition showed the population shifts from a backwards escape response to rapid forward acceleration away from the locus of stimulation

citation: Gianluca Romano, Jan Schneider, Daniele Di Mitri, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00526-1
title: Harrow's taxonomy as the review's chosen framework for classifying skill proficiency levels in ITS
description: Harrow's taxonomy (1972) classifies psychomotor skills in six levels of increasing performance capability: "Reflex Movements, Basic Fundamental Movements, Perceptual Abilities, Physical Abilities, Skilled Movements, Non-discursive Communication". The review selected it over Dave's, Simpson's, Thomas's, and Ferris and Aziz's taxonomies because it includes physical and non-discursive elements; its Physical Activities level accommodates stretching, strength, flexibility, complex sports movements, and expressive movements. The review applies it as a checklist at task level to reveal how mastery of psychomotor skills is promoted in existing ITS.
requirements: Application at task level, checking whether a task's execution corresponds to a taxonomy level, with similar tasks grouped to account for class imbalances
constraints: Dave's, Simpson's, and Ferris and Aziz's taxonomies give no possibility to classify physical or motor abilities; Thomas's taxonomy focuses on learning outcomes, making it less straightforward to apply
target_learners: Learners using ITS to develop psychomotor skills
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor skill proficiency across Harrow's levels
examples: The review classifies following basic salsa steps as covering all levels except Physical Activities, since the implemented dancing task does not require fitness despite its importance for dancing

article_title: Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY
citation: C.E. Holdich, P.W.H. Chung and R.G. Holdich. (2004). Improving children's written grammar and style: revising and editing with HARRY. Computers & Education, Vol 42, pp1-23. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/

Prompts are stored in Access databases and randomly presented so each child receives a different set.

A Windows NT web server with ASP scripts and Microsoft Access databases; children access it via a standard web browser

Revision and editing skills
Vocabulary variety and sophistication
Sentence construction variety

article_title: Hampshire Hundreds: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Sandra McNally, Amy Challen, Gill Wyness, Anne West, Philip Noden. (2014). Hampshire Hundreds Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk

description: Hampshire Hundreds was a local-authority-led intervention for Years 5 and 6 in which lead teachers attended cluster meetings, observed disadvantaged pupils using a characteristics resource, and were given research material on feedback and questioning (e.g. Hattie, 2009; 2012), being "encouraged to consider how they could adapt Hattie's model of feedback and apply it in their lessons". Schools supported additional staff time for testing, lesson observation, co-planning and responding to project data requests

reducing the attainment gap between disadvantaged pupils and their peers

title: Hard scaffolding: static advance supports that reduce free-riding and cognitive load in cooperative learning
description: The article draws on Saye and Brush's concept of hard scaffolding as 'static supports that are devised in advance based on typical student difficulties with a task', implemented here as a paper-based worksheet. It sits within a Vygotskian framing in which scaffolding enables a novice to accomplish tasks beyond unassisted efforts and peer interaction facilitates cognitive growth. The authors argue that integrating well-structured scaffolding into cooperative learning minimizes the free-rider effect and promotes individual accountability, and they cite Saye and Brush's finding that hard scaffolding decreased learners' cognitive loads and fostered more active engagement.

Support is needed more as the task becomes more complicated and student ability decreases
constraints: The article notes cooperative learning had been neither widely applied to young children nor systematically studied in EFL classrooms, motivating this population

target_learning_goals: Constructing knowledge through peer interaction
Becoming self-regulated learners

constraints: The model is presented as a theoretical framework of composing sub-processes, not as an empirically tested component of this study

Meta-analytic software such as STATA for reconfiguration

title: Hattie and Timperley's three-question feedback model
description: The article uses Hattie and Timperley's feedback model as its organising framework for what high-quality feedback addresses. The model identifies "three feedback questions, which should be addressed in order to provide high‐quality feedback: 'where am I going', 'how am I going' and 'where to next'". The EFeCT tool was chosen because it aligns with this model, and the study found the three questions were addressed the majority of the time, though 'where to next' was most often omitted.
requirements: High-quality feedback should address all three questions: where am I going, how am I going, and where to next.
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: formative feedback that enhances learning
examples: The EFeCT tool maps its five criteria onto the three feedback questions, allocating a point for context to help the learner recall the encounter.

title: Health Action Process Approach (HAPA): a self-regulation model distinguishing motivational and volitional phases of health behavior change
description: HAPA is a behavior-change model that divides health behavior change into a motivational phase, where risk awareness, outcome expectancy, and action self-efficacy shape intention, and a volitional phase, where planning, coping self-efficacy, and recovery self-efficacy convert intention into action. It distinguishes pre-intender, intender, and action stages. The article used HAPA constructs as the structure of a seven-session teaching program and credits it with bridging the intention-behavior gap: it "proposes a distinction between pre-intentional motivational processes that lead to a behavioral intention and post-intentional volitional processes that lead to actual behavior."
requirements: Teaching must address both motivational constructs (risk perception, outcome expectancy, action self-efficacy) and volitional constructs (planning, coping and recovery self-efficacy)
constraints: The article notes prior models were criticized as too general for specific subgroups; HAPA's reported effect here is limited to older, literate adults with hypertension in one Iranian health center
target_learners: Older adults (over 60) with chronic conditions such as hypertension
target_learning_goals: Adoption and maintenance of self-care behaviors (diet, medication adherence, self-monitoring, disease management)
examples: The study's seven weekly sessions each targeted one HAPA construct, from understanding risk in session one to recovery self-efficacy in session seven

article_title: Simulation training with haptic feedback of instrument vibrations reduces resident workload during live robot-assisted sleeve gastrectomy.
citation: Gomez ED, Husin HM, Dumon KR, Williams NN, Kuchenbecker KJ. (2024). Simulation training with haptic feedback of instrument vibrations reduces resident workload during live robot-assisted sleeve gastrectomy. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11459-6
title: Provide naturalistic haptic feedback of instrument vibrations during early robotic surgery simulation training to reduce trainee workload in later live operations
description: The article concludes that "it may be beneficial to utilize haptic feedback of instrument vibrations for training residents in robotic surgery", because training with such feedback during dry-lab simulation was associated with lower subjective workload both in later simulations and during subsequent live robot-assisted surgery performed without feedback. The reduction persisted after controlling for PGY level, operative time, case number, and baseline anxiety. The authors frame this as reducing workload due to novelty of the surgical device so limited cognitive reserve can focus on the procedure itself.
requirements: A vibrotactile feedback system such as VerroTouch attached to the training robot, and procedure-specific simulation sessions early in training.
constraints: Evidence comes from a single-blinded study with only six participants per group that the authors judge inadequately powered; applicability to more difficult robotic procedures and to other forms of haptic feedback is subject to further investigation.
target_learners: General surgery residents in early robotic surgery training
target_learning_goals: Reduced cognitive workload during robotic surgical skill acquisition and live operations
examples: Twelve residents were randomized to haptic or control groups; the haptic group trained with vibration feedback for four of five simulated bariatric surgeries and then showed lower NASA-TLX workload in the live OR.

correct insertion depth control using the hard-stop cue

description: The consensus recommendations hold that independent use of the compound light microscope is a mandatory skill attained through hands-on training throughout fellowship, and that learners should also understand the benefits and limitations of digital and remote microscopy. The article states "Learners should be competent in the personal use of a compound light microscope, and should receive hands on training throughout fellowship" and that manual review via light microscopy or digital whole slide imaging is strongly preferred over single high-power field images. This prepares trainees for FDA-approved WSI platforms likely to enter routine practice.

constraints: More than half of participants already use remote digital microscopy or whole slide imaging in clinical practice, so curricula must address both modalities

target_learning_goals: independent microscope-based PBS interpretation and awareness of digital microscopy workflows
examples: The recommendations include teaching identification of the monolayer, use of various magnifications, and awareness of limitations of digital and remote microscopy
